opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. It's a great question, because there's a real gap between a model that produces impressive 3D output in a research setting and something a person actually wants to use every day.

The first challenge is that 3D is fundamentally harder than language or 2D images. Language is a one-dimensional signal, and we've gotten very good at modeling it. But the physical world is three-dimensional, governed by physics, geometry, and light. A model has to respect things like object permanence, occlusion, and consistent structure when you move the camera. If any of that breaks, users notice right away, because our visual systems have been trained over hundreds of millions of years of evolution to detect when something isn't right in space.

The second challenge is data. We don't have an internet's worth of clean 3D data the way we have text. So much of the work is figuring out how to learn spatial understanding from images, video, and simulation, and then making that output reliable enough for real workflows.

Third, and this is the product side, is meeting people where they are. Creators, game developers, architects, roboticists all have existing tools and pipelines. A beautiful generated world doesn't help if you can't edit it, export it, or control it. Controllability and interactivity matter as much as raw quality. People don't just want to look at a world; they want to step into it, change it, and build on it.

And finally there's speed and cost. 3D generation is computationally heavy, and for something to feel like a creative tool rather than a batch job, it has to be responsive.

What keeps me excited is that spatial intelligence is so foundational. Seeing leads to doing. If we get this right, it unlocks not just creative applications but robotics, design, education, and ways for humans and machines to share an understanding of the world we live in.

r001.rationale: It describes the physical world as three-dimensional and names the gap between impressive research output and something people use every day, conveying the difficulty of making ubiquitous 3D usable.

r002.rationale: It says people want to step into, change, and build on 3D worlds rather than merely look at them, but it does not contrast that with active engagement through language.

fable-5.1.text:
I'll answer directly as the guest.

You know, it's a great question, because I think the honest answer is that we're earlier than people assume. Language models had this incredible advantage: the internet handed them trillions of tokens of human-generated text, already structured, already carrying meaning. The 3D world didn't give us that gift. There's no "internet of 3D." So before you even get to product, you're confronting a data problem that's fundamentally harder, and a representation problem too. What is the right way to even represent a world? Is it a mesh, a point cloud, a neural field, something we haven't named yet? We're still arguing about the alphabet.

Then there's the gap between something that looks right and something that is right. In an image, if the lighting is a little off, your eye forgives it. In 3D, the moment a person moves the camera, or a robot tries to put its hand on an object, every inconsistency shows up. Geometry has to be coherent, physics has to hold, objects have to persist when you look away and look back. Humans are brutally good at noticing when a world is broken, because we've spent hundreds of millions of years of evolution being sensitive to exactly that. So the bar for "usable" is much higher than the bar for "impressive demo."

And the last thing I'd say is about the users themselves. Who actually needs this? Game designers, architects, filmmakers, roboticists, scientists. They don't want a magic black box. They want control. They want to say, move that wall, change that material, make the chair heavier. So the challenge isn't just generating a world, it's making it editable and reliable enough that a professional will trust it in their workflow. That's where the research meets reality, and it's humbling. But it's also why I find it so exciting. Spatial intelligence is, to me, the next frontier, and the hard parts are exactly the parts worth doing.

r001.rationale: It says 3D is harder to productize than people assume and describes data, representation, and reliability challenges, but does not identify the paradox that 3D is ubiquitous in everyday experience yet difficult to deliver as a usable consumer product.

r002.rationale: It discusses professional users wanting control and editable worlds, but does not contrast active engagement through language with passively viewing 3D content.

astra-6.text:
I think one of the biggest challenges is the gap between generating something that looks compelling and generating something that people can actually use. With 3D, that gap is substantial. You can show a beautiful view of a room, but what happens when you move around it? Does the geometry make sense? Can you change an object while keeping the rest of the space consistent?

And the requirements depend on the user. A game developer needs something different from an architect or a roboticist. So you have to understand the workflow: What does this person want to create? How much control do they need? How does the result fit into the tools they already use?

That’s what makes this so interesting. The model is a foundation, but the product has to give people a way to express intent, iterate, and trust what they’re building. A beautiful demo is a beginning; making it useful requires that whole loop.

r001.rationale: The response describes a gap between compelling 3D visuals and usable products, but does not say that 3D is ubiquitous in everyday experience yet difficult to deliver as a consumer product.

r002.rationale: It contrasts viewing a beautiful room with interacting with or changing it, but does not contrast language-based active engagement with passive viewing.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one challenge is that a 3D model is not, by itself, a product. You have to ask: Who is using it, and what are they trying to do? If you’re a designer, you probably don’t just want something that looks compelling from one viewpoint. You want to move around it, change it, and have those changes behave consistently.

That puts a lot of demands on the technology. You need spatial consistency, controllability, and a way to interact that feels intuitive. Most people don’t want to learn a whole technical vocabulary just to express what they have in mind.

So I think the work is really connecting the capability of the model to a human workflow. Can someone take an idea, explore it, revise it, and get something useful? That’s a much richer problem than generating a beautiful demonstration.

r001.rationale: The response says a 3D model is not itself a product and describes usability challenges, but does not identify 3D as ubiquitous in everyday experience or frame that as a paradox.

r002.rationale: It contrasts viewing from one viewpoint with moving around and changing a model, but does not describe language as the means of active engagement.
